speechtext:
I will not take long. I want to refer to one or two statements made by the Minister of Finance on September 12, 1939, regarding a pay-as-you-go policy. He said:
	as I have already said, the real costs
of war must come out of current production, out of the goods and services produced during the war. It is true that some stocks of military supplies may be on hand at the beginning of a war, but their importance is slight for a war of any duration ....
First of all let me emphasize that however we finance the cost of the war, whether by taxation or by borrowing or by inflation, we cannot escape its real costs. By the real costs I mean the goods and services which have to be sacrificed out of our current production to meet the needs of war.
.... and I repeat it again, that in real terms, namely, in terms of the loss to the nation of this production, a war is paid for substantially during its duration.
I am afraid that the minister at that time was indulging in wishful thinking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I was stating a fact; I was not announcing a policy.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The minister admitted that the real cost of war was substantially paid for during the war. If that is so, why cannot its financial cost also be met during the war? I will put it to him in this way. We must
War Appropriation Bill

admit that while we are prepared to pay the real cost of the war, in so far as goods are concerned, we are not prepared to pay the financial cost; that is to say, a certain class of society is not prepared to make the sacrifice which is necessary in order that such a policy may be adopted. If they were, there would be no increase in debt apart from that resulting from the sale of war savings certificates. What we are really saying is this, that while we are providing the goods to prosecute this war, we are going to demand that future generations shall compensate us for a large proportion of this production. And remember that by far the greatest proportion of that compensation will be paid to a comparatively few people.
I cannot understand how anyone can say that that is an honest policy; for what is the government really doing? It is misappropriating the funds of future generations. Some people may attempt to justify such a policy on the ground that we are fighting a war to make the world safe for democracy for future generations, and that, therefore, future generations should be prepared to pay a certain proportion of the cost of the war. I heard the same sort of statement made time and again from 1914 to 1918. I heard it said that we were fighting to make the world safe for democracy, that we were fighting the war that would end war; yet here we are to-day, twenty-five years later, engaged in one of the greatest wars the world has ever known.
No; I do not think we have any right to ask future generations to sacrifice themselves for the troubles that we are facing to-day, because I believe that future generations will have plenty of troubles of their own without having to look after ours, as we are having to take care of troubles that were incurred hundreds of years ago. Britain is still paying interest in connection with the Crimean war, and in connection with every major war fought in the last hundred years or so. It is high time we started a real pay-as-you-go policy, because it would not entail a reduction in the standard of living of the people to a level lower than that due to the present policy of the government; whereas the difference that would be brought about would be this, that people would not have as a result of the war, at the end of the war, large accumulations of bonds representing nothing more or less than war profiteering. I say again, therefore, that there is no justification for the attempt to pass on any large proportion of the financial cost of the war to future generations.
I do not suppose it will do any good to ask the Minister of Finance again to consider this question. I appreciate the fact that he

has been quite frank in answering a number of questions, but before sitting down I should like to put to him a few more very short questions, which I think he can answer easily without deep consideration. Can he explain why rates of interest on money borrowed from the chartered banks vary? Why does the interest rate on money borrowed from the chartered banks since the declaration of war vary as it does? In one instance, it is two per cent; in another, one and a half per cent.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister was kind enough to answer a question which I placed on the order paper some time ago in connection with interest-free bonds. I was delighted to see that the Canadian public had responded in a very generous manner, but I was surprised to learn that the minister's department had spent only something like $600 in popularizing this type of saving. Perhaps the minister would make a statement about the possibility of spending additional sums of money to try to promote the sale of bonds of this type.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It is not the policy of the government to promote the sale of interest-free bonds by campaigns of advertising, or the like. That policy was decided upon after a great deal of consideration. As to whether it is a right or a wrong policy, I never have been sure. I believe that in England1 they ask the public to buy interest-free bonds, and they also ask the public to make donations to the government. It was felt in this country, however, that if we started advertising campaigns. which cost a lot of money, and otherwise promoted in a wide-spread manner the sale of interest-free bonds, the result would be that the conscientious, generous and self-sacrificing part of the population would perhaps be buying interest-free bonds as a matter of duty, and the more selfish or prudent part of the population would be buying the bonds which carried interest. It was thought that we would be open to severe criticism. It would be suggested that there was not that equality of sacrifice about which we have been talking. Therefore, when we have asked the public to buy bonds, it has always been in connection with bonds which pay interest. We make it clear, however, to any persons who wish to buy interest-free bonds as a matter of patriotic duty, that we deeply appreciate their action, and we make the particulars with respect to those bonds available. Also, when persons send us donations-and there are thousands of people who make gifts to the government-we do not discourage them. We are very grateful for those donations, and appreciate the spirit which prompts them. We offer our thanks for such donations, but we do not go out and advertise for them.
It is open to the committee to express its views as to that policy; but if we took the other one, I am afraid hon. members in the group which has been addressing itself to this matter would be the first to criticize it by saying that the long-headed and shrewd part of the population were lending their money at fairly good rates of interest, while we were trying to force these bonds on the more unselfish and self-sacrificing part of the popu-

lation. It would be suggested that there could be no equality in a programme like that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Has the minister not presented a good argument for compulsory interest-free loans? That is what he has done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Perhaps I presented one argument. I believe, however, other arguments against compulsory loans would outweigh the one I have presented. The hon. member knows that other considerations enter into the matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I believe all hon. members who are at present in the chamber will benefit in some degree from the discussion which has taken place this afternoon. The results that may flow from it will no doubt be seen in the days which follow. I believe the people of Canada are interested in seeing that as light a burden of debt as possible be placed upon the coming generation. We do not want another crop of millionaires lining their pockets with tax-free bonds, as they did after the last war.
I do not offer any excuse this afternoon for having taken time of the committee in discussing this measure. We are considering a resolution which would permit the expenditure of $1,300,000,000. If we continue as we have been doing, it will be $2,600,000,000 next year and $5,000,000,000 in the third year. If our programme of shipbuilding alone is to be continued until 1945, I feel quite sure that anyone who knows anything about elementary arithmetic will realize that the debt structure we shall have in Canada after this war will not stand the burden. Every realistic person realizes that wre are going to need a new set of rules. The seed that is destroying the present system is the seed of interest. It may bring down our whole financial structure after the war is over, and there are a great many parts of that financial structure which I believe most of the people will be glad to get rid of.

I wish to refer briefly to a matter brought to the attention of the committee a few nights ago. I refer to the matter of health. Apparently we need men to man our aeroplanes. These are figures which Canada must face. I quote from the words of the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) at page 1605-6 of Hansard:
There will be for training this year 93,000 young men of the age of twenty-one years.
Without hesitation one can knock off 33 per cent of those as being unfit even for military training camps.
That is, 30,000 of these men would be unfit even for military training camps. To continue:
That is, they would be placed in classes C-l or C, and unfit to walk five miles.
What a glorious tribute to the health of Canada's youth!
They are completely eliminated, so far as the air force is concerned. Then, the difference between C and A-plus, with good eyesight, would mean that one would knock off another 30,000, leaving about 30,000 annually from which we can draw.
Then, if one looks at them from the point of view of educational qualifications I believe he would knock off another half of those-these would be the ones -who have not high-school matriculation-leaving 15,000 eligibles.
One man in six, the flower of Canada's manhood, men in the prime of life, twenty-one years of age! What is happening to the health of Canada? What has happened in the past? Perhaps these facts will shock the Canadian people from some of their apathy. They reveal that the health problem in Canada is a real one. It is urgent, and I want to know why it is neglected. It is closely linked up with the matter of education, and I think it has arisen from neglect, poverty, insecurity and bad housing conditions. If the facts were given to the Canadian people with regard to present housing conditions in Canada, I am sure we would hang our heads in shame. Bad housing is where crime and vice breed. That is where a nation declines. We are at war, and yet we find that only one man in six who is examined is fit to be a pilot. A poverty stricken, ignorant and unhealthy populace fits in well with the plans of certain European dictatorships. Such people are easily frightened and easily bribed. You can drive such a populace wherever you will, like frightened sheep. I maintain that in Canada we have no room for a populace which is unhealthy, ignorant or poverty stricken. Such conditions have no place in Canada's economy. The right to health in this country should be as readily recognizable as the right to breathe. What kind of country are we building? I want to know who is responsible for these conditions. Is it political expediency that allows such conditions to exist? Have we a department of health?
Looking over the membership of the house, I find that there are seventeen medical doctors -fifteen on the government side, and I believe two on the opposition side. There are at least a dozen laymen like myself who are willing to help, but we seem to be blocked at every step we try to take. I inquired last July whether there would be a committee on health. That was in the closing days
War Appropriation Bill

when the estimates were before the house, and I was informed that the matter was under consideration-that is the usual answer. I asked again in December what was going to happen in this matter, and I was told that a voluntary committee of members of the house was set up. I was a member of that committee, and I can say that it was set up only for the purpose of trying to get action from the government in attacking this problem of health. But such action was not taken. When I inquired again in February of this year I was told that the minister did not intend to set up a parliamentary committee on health.
Nevertheless there is much work to be done. There is the matter of research. Perhaps research would reveal more startling facts regarding the health of the Canadian people which would not make very good reading, and if the statement which I saw in the Montreal Gazette this morning by a member of the provincial legislature of Quebec is true, there are some startling health facts which the people of Canada should know. This question needs publicity. We need cooperation between the health departments of the provinces and health organizations right across Canada, and the Department of Pensions and National Health in this government should be correlating and bringing together, the various schemes of the provincial departments of health. Splendid work is being done by provincial recreation centres in British Columbia and by the antituberculosis league in Saskatchewan. Why not extend such efforts? This matter is closely linked up with education. We need a proper national viewpoint, and this house should be giving that leadership on the question. We are paying to-day for our failure in the past to attack this problem. We need men now who are strong, virile and healthy. I am sorry the Minister of Pensions and National Health has left his seat, but I suppose the financial questions which have been discussed this afternoon have wearied him.

Mr. Chairman,
the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said before the dinner recess that we on this side should be satisfied with the way in which this debate has been carried on. because it was the method which Sir

War Appropriation BUI
Robert Borden used in times gone by. I took the trouble to look up Hansard of 1917 and 1918, and I found that there is quite a lot of difference. In 1917 Sir Robert Borden introduced a similar resolution in the House of Commons, and immediately started in and gave the full details of the estimates for 1914-15, 1915-16, 1916-17, and then the war estimates for the then current year. That was the procedure followed; there was a great deal of detail, and several other ministers spoke at that time.
In 1918 the resolution was introduced by the Hon. J. D. Reid, who, in introducing it, said:
I may say that an understanding was arrived at between the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition to the effect that the statement which is necessary to be made in connection with the resolution should be made on the second reading of the bill. It was decided between them that this resolution should be allowed to go through and a bill founded upon it introduced.
There was very little discussion about it. But what happened was that by mutual consent the resolution was allowed to go through. Then on April 10, Sir Robert Borden gave a full and detailed account of all the expenditures theretofore and the appropriations which would be necessary for that year for the carrying on of the war.
Even though the Minister of National Defence thinks the present procedure is good enough for us because of what was done by Sir Robert Borden, the resolution moved by Sir Robert Borden was for $500,000,000, which was a lot of money in those days, yet it was not quite on the same scale, either in vastness of amount or in the detail connected with it, as the resolution now before us, and it seems to me that the government should have taken a little more care to have the debate carried on in an orderly fashion. If the important point was to get the appropriation through quickly so that the government would have the money required to carry on with, there can be no question that, with the consent of the house, a proportion of the money could have been voted, just as for years we have voted a proportion of the estimates. Further, it would have been very easy to have had a book prepared giving in detail by departments all the estimated expenditures, without the necessity of having the ministers stay in their places and repeat the details to the committee. Had this material been printed, hon. members would have had an opportunity of studying it.
I admit that there has been a little delay, and possibly some repetition. On the other hand, under the system involved in this resolution, hon. members, who cannot be in their
places all the time, may miss something, when it is brought up in this unorderly way, if they happen to be out of the chamber, and that naturally leads to repetition and loss of time. Had they had the estimates to study, much delay would have been avoided.
On the other hand, the last thing in our minds-in mine, anyway-is to delay anything. A plan such as I have outlined, whereby the estimates would go through without the necessity of ministers attending other than the minister in charge of the particular department, would save members of the cabinet a great deal of time.
It must be pointed out that our constituents are interested in knowing how this money is being spent. They want to know what has been going on. They want to know what progress is being made. It is our duty, even in times like these, to find these things out. The $700,000,000 which we voted last fall went through with hardly a murmur. Now, it seems to me, the people of the country are entitled to some details of the expenditures.
In connection with certain financial aspects of this resolution, for example matters affecting companies which are in receipt of capital assistance, the banking and commerce committee could be properly asked to investigate and find out what has happened, where there are no secrets concerned. I am sure that the public would be well satisfied if all material facts were brought to the light of day.
I suggest that, in future, some course such as I have outlined should be followed, and I do not think it is too late now to do something of the kind. Certain elements of these war expenditure estimates have not yet been accounted for: for example, items with respect to the post office, the national revenue-a small item, it is true-and fisheries. Possibly, when we get into committee on the bill, some such arrangement could be adopted.

I should like to discuss a few matters affecting the Department of National War Services. I am sure that all hon. members were interested in the description the minister gave some days ago with regard to the national registration, and I have no doubt that hon. members have been greatly concerned about the large numbers of people in the various constituencies in Canada who are still waiting anxiously for directions as to where they may find employment in the different war industries. The minister, speaking on Tuesday of this week, said that for some reason or another a great many people now think they should make application to Ottawa and they write to some minister or to some person connected with the promotion of some particular industry. He said:
We simply had to advise them that all the information with regard to these matters is now, as it always has been, at the labour offices and that that is the proper place to apply; that they can get action quicker in that way than by applying to someone else somewhere else.
The difficulty in Saskatchewan is that the labour offices find it next to impossible to direct people seeking employment to places where they might find it. I had some experience with the employment office at Yorkton last year when the air training school was under construction. On one occasion I was told that there were some 700 employees on the waiting list, and one of our difficulties has been that apparently we have no machinery set up to make it possible for the unemployed to move from one part of Canada to another.
The minister, writing from Ottawa on July 27, said:
We hope to be able to help the Canadian people by means of the information gathered -to direct those presently unemployed to employment, and to aid those who are employed in obtaining more gainful employment.
I realize that there are difficulties in carrying out an objective of that sort, but the letter was written on July 27 and I think the department should be able to report by now some progress in that direction. Hoping that some machinery would be set up by November,
I wrote to the associate minister stating that I had received a letter from the secretary of the Pelly branch of the Canadian Legion in connection with finding employment for the daughters of one of the veterans of the last war, one girl aged twenty-five and the other nineteen, and that I wondered if he could give me information as to where and when employment might be found. The associate deputy minister replied, saying:
I would strongly suggest that (the) two daughters write to the secretary of the commission and secure applications.
The reference was to the civil service commission.
They should complete the same and return them. Thus they will be in line for employment in the future as and when further employees are being sought.
I discussed the matter with the secretary of the civil service commission and was advised that it would be misleading to these girls to encourage them to make application to the civil service commission because at present they had no machinery for the placing of girls who were not stenographers or had no other special qualifications. Therefore, on the advice of the secretary of the civil service commission I did not carry out that suggestion.
The associate deputy minister went on to say:
I have had a good many letters from people in the west with special qualifications amply fitting them for employment in war industries, and I have suggested to them that they go to their nearest employment office, register thereat, and ask the manager of the office to communicate with the employment offices in the larger industrial centres of Canada. These offices are pretty well informed as to where employment is to be found. In this way they do bring together those seeking employment and those seeking employees.
The letter went on to say:
The whole problem is very much to the fore at the moment, and I know is being thoroughly canvassed and considered by the Department of Labour and the national labour supply board. It will also be given consideration by the minister of this department, the Hon. Mr. Gardiner, on his return from Great Britain.

That letter was dated November 6. The difficulty seems to be that we have not any machinery that will enable the people seeking employment, in Saskatchewan for example, where we have no war industries operating at the present time, to get in touch with industries in Ontario or Quebec. The minister mentioned the other night that they have machinery here, so that manufacturers wishing employees could find out where properly qualified people might be found, and I am sure that a valuable piece of work is being done in that connection. I should like, however, to ask what machinery we have for keeping these cards up to date. The registration took place last August. Is there an up to date record as to which of those registered as unemployed last year now have employment, so that manufacturers who wish to secure toolmakers, for example, or steel workers, could obtain the names of those who were unemployed in that particular industry and know whether or not they are now working? Further, what progress is being made towards directing the unemployed to where they might find employment in other parts of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think the system under which the direction is given is pretty well outlined in the letter written by the associate deputy minister. In the first place, as I stated the other night, there is in the statistics branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce, which is doing this work now at the request of the war services department, a list of persons across Canada who are capable of doing certain kinds of work. So far as industries that require that type of labour are concerned, there is no difficulty; they can make application to the department and get lists from any part of Canada they desire, and with those lists they can make inquiry and engage as many of those persons as they require.
When the initiative is taken by the industry, the machinery is to be found in the lists that are available. As to keeping the lists up to date, an effort is made to do that. That effort will not be entirely successful unless there is one hundred per cent cooperation on the part of those looking for jobs; that is, if they move from one place to another, they should notify the branch keeping the lists. An attempt is being made to get that done, but it may not be done quite one hundred per cent.
On the other hand, individuals desiring to find employment should as far as possible follow the advice that was given by the associate deputy minister; that is, they should use the machinery which has been set up by

the Department of Labour at Ottawa, cooperating with the labour branches in the different provinces, by listing their names with the labour offices. It is assumed that if they request that that be done, those names will be filed at the centres where industry is situated and where employees may be required. In so far as that is done, I think the machinery makes it possible to bring the unemployed person in touch with the industry where employment is available.
Further, I do not think it is impossible for the individual to get service by writing direct to the labour offices in the larger districts and seeing that their names are filed there. In other words, it is to be assumed that the individual will do everything possible on his part. I know that most are anxious to do that, but they often do not know just how to proceed. If we as members, when we get communications from individuals seeking work, would try to instruct them along that line, sooner or later the greater number would at least know how to make use of the machinery that is available. We are putting out information regarding it from time to time, but I am afraid it does not always reach those desiring it.
I do not think there is anything I can add so far as the machinery set up is concerned. I am doubtful whether we could set up machinery that would be any more complete. We might change the administration from one department to another and get more of it into one place, but it is a question whether that would produce any better results.
The other difficulty referred to by the hon. member was that of persons getting from where they are to the place where employment might be found. The information that I have is that with regard to most of those who are requiring employees, that is in connection with war industries or shipbuilding, when they have been able to locate persons suitable for their employment there has not been any great difficulty in having funds advanced to take them from where they are to the place of employment. The main difficulty is, I think, to convince the industry that the individual is qualified to do the work so that it will take the chance of paying the transportation. It would probably be just as difficult to get government bodies to do the same thing. We have, of course, the additional difficulty that there may be a certain amount of unemployment in a province, and if persons were to be moved into that province from another one, the provincial government would probably have to be consulted. The machinery, however, is there, making it possible to bring about the contact. It may be it is not sufficiently generally known that the machinery is provided.

It is unfortunate that a great many people between the ages of forty and fifty and even between fifty and sixty, who found themselves unemployed during the period of depression, are finding the greatest difficulty in getting back into employment again. I regret, as I am sure every other hon.

It may be that younger people could do the work to better advantage, but there may be some other work to be done by younger people that older people can not do, and in such instances it might be necessary to urge the employment of many of those who were on those lists made up under the voluntary effort. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It seems to me that we in this house are in danger of overdoing the slogan, "This time we are all in the front line." With all proper respect to the author of those words, so far as Canada is concerned they simply are not true. It is not only untrue that we are all in the front line in Canada; unhappily it is true also that many of us apparently have not realized the magnitude of our task, which is to get on with the battle itself. It is now a month since we began to deal with this resolution, and perhaps *we should note that it is not taking nearly so long to deal with the seven billion dollar appropriation which is being discussed in Washington to-night.
This debate has lagged disgracefully. It is a spectacle that reflects no credit upon either the earnestness or the sincerity of any of us in this house. To emphasize in its defence the importance of opposition is to insult the intelligence of all, and does not fool anybody. The word "break-down", I think, has become almost overworked during this discussion; I believe if we took out that one word we would save a day or two. The break-down, if there has been a break-down in this house, has been the break-down of the opposition which, bankrupt of ideas, keeps bobbing up, hinting this and insinuating that. As a result of this procedure, two conditions have arisen in this house and in the country. In the first place, unthinking criticism has had and is having the effect of widening the gap between the government and the public, or perhaps it would be better to say the gap between parliament and the public; and this at the very time when public confidence is essential to victory. The second result of this recognized weakness has been that the newspapers of the country have been led to attempt to usurp the function of opposition, to become the thoughtful, informed critics of the administration. Apropos of that
War Appropriation Bill

situation, I should like with your permission, Mr. Chairman, to recall the words of a very wise American editor, now dead, who said: "A government without newspapers would be intolerable. A government with newspapers is endurable. A government by newspapers would be the worst conceivable."
Linked' with the folly of criticism without regard to ultimate consequences is another evil which is sometimes evidenced in this house. We have been told how difficult it is for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. Sometimes I have thought that a camel passing through the eye of a needle would have an easy time compared with the problem of a cabinet minister admitting an error in judgment. This chamber has been called the last refuge of free speech, and that has not been a jocular reference. There is real reason to agree with the thought that in this country it is the last refuge of free speech. But that does not justify or excuse licence in connection with this forum. We have been singularly free from licence, in the sense of misuse of our privileges, but this does bring me to one or two conclusions.
The first conclusion to which I have come is that in this country we have been a bit silly about censorship. I do not think any real harm has been done, but personally I object to the banning of publications because they hold views which are unpopular or not in accordance with those of the majority of us. I protest against that sort of thing; in my opinion it is a violation of the rights of the citizen. I do not think it heals any breaches in public opinion. I think it accomplishes no worth while end. Our cause

the cause of the government, of parliament, of the country and of the empire-is a just one; I think we can justify ourselves both at home and in the eyes of the world with regard to our methods of protecting the system of society in which most of us still believe and have a good deal of confidence, without resorting to the very practices against which we are fighting at the present time. I should like to make it perfectly clear that I am referring not to military censorship, but rather to the type of censorship which is aimed at things, written or oral, with which the majority of us happen to disagree.
Even I know the exasperation which comes from attempting to answer carping criticism. Most of us, perhaps, have not the consciousness of virtue which cloaks almost all governments-and I suppose always will-like a mantle; but even you and I would sometimes choke off thoughtless criticism if we dared or if we had the opportunity. I think we all need the criticism of both friend and foe in

order to retain our proper perspective, and in any event, to my mind this is the essence of the democratic principle.
This unreality of the proceedings here during the last' month or so; this failure to face up to our situation, as evidenced by our deeds rather than by our words, has come as a shock to people outside the house. I have no hesitation in saying that the atmosphere which pervaded this house during the first ten days of our participation in this war was something which will not be forgotten by anyone who had the privilege of experiencing it. A good deal of that has, it seems to me, evaporated somewhere in the meantime. And in spite of the example of those in other lands who have been lulled by temporary inaction we are following the same fatal practice here, and trying to do business as usual. It occurs to me that with respect to the debate on this resolution, in particular, the government is not to blame. With praiseworthy promptness the resolution was put before us. We may haggle about the method of it and the phraseology of it, or the general practice with respect to it, but the fact remains that within forty-eight hours of the time we arrived here we had an opportunity to begin our deliberations.
We the members of the House of Commons in all parties are those who are responsible for delay. Our people are willing and anxious to be led to greater things than any inspiration they can get from this last month in the House of Commons would justify. Every day since I first came to this chamber in 1936 I have had the opportunity to sit on the opposition side of the house. And during the last days I have been here I am bound to say I have been more comfortable about it than I had ever been during the previous time. I am not paying tribute to any changes or to any newcomer on this side of the house, when I say that. But, disturbed as I am about what I conceive to be the unreality of our attitude, it is worth something to me to be able to sit on this side of the house day by day and to be able to look into the face of the one man who, I am sure, has looked into the future with eyes undimmed by false hopes and without being motivated by pious wishes. I seek the opportunity to say that because I believe it represents not only the view which is my own, but the view of those whom it is my privilege to represent.
We have been rather tender about mentioning polities in the last little while, except to mention it by suggestion or innuendo, as something which is a bit discreditable. In connection with that I have a word or two I should like to say. There is a form of political brigandage which is not confined to the east

War Appropriation Bill
or to the west, and which is not entirely confined to political parties. It creeps sometimes into organizations of persons who have banded themselves together for purposes other than the promotion of the government of the country. I do not care whether that type of propaganda-politics-is cloaked in the verbal garb of patriotism or whether it comes out openly as a kind of self promotion; it is something which should be scotched. No dignity should be lent to it by taking it into consideration in the deliberations of this chamber.
I wonder whether we have so soon forgotten the spirit of sacrifice that built this country? I wonder whether no one does any more dedicate himself or herself to the task which is ours with something of the fine fervour of the Jesuit fathers, the covenanting Scot, the Puritan pilgrims or the huguenots? Men starved and froze, strained every nerve and tissue to make this country what it is and to win the privileges which we have, to the protection of which we all give lip-service in between bouts of seeking our own selfish ends.
Some excuse themselves on this account from greater service on the plea that there is in the war effort inequality of sacrifice. There awcr was and there never will be equality of sacrifice with respect either to the war effort or to any of those problems or those efforts which require sacrifice. Sacrifice is not something which can be measured in a measuring cup, or with a yardstick. Sacrifice involves- if it means anything at all-giving all an individual has. Fortunately or unfortunately, all are not equally endowed.
Let me repeat that equality of sacrifice is an objective always to keep in mind, bearing with that thought the realization that there is not any common yardstick for measuring it. In debates such as this, and in consideration of problems such as we are now considering, it has become a political catch-phrase, the cloak of the demagogue and those who imitate him.
At this point I should like to say a word or two about questions which have been asked during this session. In my opinion, most of the questions which have been asked in the house concerning the military efforts of Canada were improper questions. And I make bold to say that at least some of the answers which were made were at least indiscreet. The first reason I believe for the asking of improper questions arises out of an honest desire to understand what is taking place. Perhaps in some instances some of us ask questions in the hope that by asking our questions we may give the impression that we understand something which, in fact, we do not understand. Generally speaking, I fancy the real reason
is an honest seeking after information. The question-harassed minister perhaps cannot resist the chance to give some credit to 'his hard-pressed staff, who are seldom offered anything in the way of praise. If they have accomplished something worth while, the temptation must be great to give some credit, because no one would assume that the minister had done it all himself. Perhaps under those circumstances we sometimes hear too much.
I fancy only a fool would try to guess what issues will predominate at the next election in Canada. That being the situation, I am at a loss to understand a good deal of the delay we have had in this debate. I am not so foolish that I cannot understand honest questioning and serious debate, but I have heard a good deal which I believe frankly was not serious, and I have read more of it than I have heard. If we admit, and we must admit, that we do not know what is going to be our problem in three or four or five years from now, I cannot see the point of spending so much time in raising little issues which the whirlwind of the next two or three months or the next two or three years will cany into oblivion-possibly with some of us, ourselves. But there is an issue which is conceivable, namely, the preservation of this chamber and the system it stands for. Every idle word spoken now, every utterance of political clap-trap and every careless word that mars the mutual understanding and cooperation of all elements in this country and in this chamber will be turned against those who in that day champion the cause of parliamentary and representative government.
If there are failures and follies in the war effort of this country-and there are; I do not think anyone denies that-we have an opportunity, and many have taken it, of going directly to the minister or the ministers who are responsible, and placing the situation before them. After all, they are the only people who can do anything about it. I say it ill becomes anyone who professes to be interested in promoting that effort to pin medals on his own breast for discovering the fault, when our real and earnest endeavour should be to draw the fault to the attention of those who are responsible, in order that the machinery may be perfected.
By the same token it seems to me that those who accept responsibility in a time like this should not regard criticism as sacrilege. Our problems are a bit too serious to let personal considerations on either side of the question enter into it at this time. I might venture a word of warning, and perhaps one of advice, since I am not one in the habit of
War Appropriation Bill

taking either. The pressure of war administration and the hand of time will too shortly, as most of us believe, deplete the ranks of those schooled in the practices of government, and steeped in the traditions of our parliamentary system. It is time those in authority began to train in the school of experience-and I do not mean just the government; I mean those of all parties who are interested in the preservation of our institutions-some who will be called upon to carry a share of the load, some who may be trained in the school of experience to meet the problems which will come. It is putting too much on Providence to believe that we can simply coast along through this war period and go through whatever is coming afterwards, and that the Lord will look after everything and raise up properly trained people to take care of the situation. I might illustrate my thought by referring to my immediate neighbours to my left. Certainly no one would say that the Conservative party is a godless party, but yet at this very moment it is a headless party, by its own admission. That is not due to Providence but partly due, at all events, to the improvidence of the party itself. That is something we might well think about.
As a Liberal who does not believe that the Liberal party has a monopoly of all grace; as a staunch believer in the two-party system; and as a sincere Canadian, I pray for the emergence of the sort of opposition which with watchful eye and helping hand will press onward with the government in order that we may speedily win the victory upon which the survival of all of us depends.
The hardest lesson which we have to learn, and some never learn it, is that war alters all values. We all need to remember that a decision which is or may be regarded as bad politics should be taken cheerfully by each and every one of us if we honestly believe it is in the interest of our common aim which is victory. By the same token, it borders on treason, just for the sake of winning some political or personal advantage, to destroy public confidence at a time when so much sacrifice is asked of those by whose grace we happen to be here.
Some day this government will disappear. It will be defeated. That is a situation which I think Canada can face with a reasonable degree of equanimity. Some day our Conservative colleagues will form a government, and I believe that Canada will survive even that. But the thing we must above all be afraid of and avoid is the failure of our free institutions of government themselves to survive. I am of opinion that by our action here, or perhaps by our words and lack of

action, something is being done to destroy the confidence of our people in those institutions which we should be doing everything to uphold. Parliament as an institution is in the hands of its members, and when some of us forget that, we all suffer for it.
Finally, referring back to what I said before, I think we should all question the wisdom of the slogan that now we are all in the front line. I think that breeds a sort of atmosphere among our people which I do not think is helpful. And growing out of that, I would say that the sons, brothers, mothers, sisters, wives and sweethearts of our soldiers, sailors and airmen, and our men themselves, have a right to expect us to match in some measure the sacrifices which they themselves so freely make.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for the last few weeks the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) has been having a fairly easy time in this house, although I have no doubt that he has been more than doing his bit outside. To-night I should like to ask him a question wTith regard to the guest children coming from Great Britain to Canada. I see in the war appropriation estimate the sum of $214,800 which is earmarked to cover "expenses re British evacuee children." We have been reading in the press during the last few days, how badly the people of Great Britain are being bombed, with an increasing number of casualties which no doubt include many children.
In the annual report of the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the last calendar year, at page 8, I find:
The total number of applications from British parents exceeded 70,000 up to July 5, 1940, when postponement of the scheme had to be announced, due to the difficulty in securing convoyed shipping space.
The report goes on to say:
On September 20, 24,130 children had been approved for Canada; 1,538 had actually sailed.
In other words, there are about 23,000 British children who have been approved for passage to Canada but have not been able to come out. The British children who have already come to Canada have won the hearts of the Canadian people. They have been more than welcome, and I believe that there are thousands and thousands of Canadian homes open now for children from Great Britain but unable to get the children. Some one has said that as many as 60,000 children could be placed. I think that just at this time it would cheer the people of Great Britain very much if this house could show beyond any question that we are only too anxious to welcome and take care of every single British child who can be brought to

War Appropriation Bill
this country. I would ask the minister to
make a statement with regard to this matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It is quite true, Mr. Chairman, that the committee has heard nothing from me so far in this debate. I would not, however, want the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) to get the impression that it has been altogether a pleasure to me to listen for four weeks to a discussion on this appropriation bill ranging over almost every subject that one could imagine. We have had monetary theories expounded, opinions given as to how the war could be won, discussions on the merits and demerits of lignite and bituminous coal, as well as the discussion of a great many other subjects as I have observed with much interest, when I have been listening to the debate.
On the subject of British guest children which has been raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South, he has, I think, stated the pertinent facts pretty well in quoting the extract he read a moment ago. As I recall it, between 1,500 and 1,600 of assisted passage British children have reached Canadian shores. In addition, there were several thousand, as I recall, approximately 5,000, who, some with their parents and some without their parents, found their way to Canada without any assistance from either the British or the Canadian government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Did the minister say 5,000?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes; my recollection is that it was about 5,000. I give that figure with reservation because I do not recall the exact number, and as I said a moment ago, between 1,500 and 1,600 of assisted passage children came out under arrangements made between the two governments. The movement started in the latter part of last summer and continued for several weeks, but as the autumn closed in and the danger of transport across the ocean increased, the British government of its own volition suspended the movement for the winter months. So far as we are aware, it was the intention of the British government to resume the movement with the coming of spring. It will, however, be in the minds of every hon. member, I am sure, that the risks to-day are even greater than they were a year ago, and consequently the British government and the British parents who might wish to send their children to a safe haven in Canada have to make a very difficult and tortured decision as to whether it is safer to keep the children in Britain, subjected as they are to bombing, or to take the risks of transferring them across the Atlantic, where they may be subjected to submarine attack. Consequently,
it is not for the Canadian government to advise the British government as to what they should do under these circumstances. The people of Britain are the best judges.
There is no misunderstanding in the minds of the British government or the British people as to the willingness of the Canadian government and the Canadian people to give asylum to all the children they can send to this country. That has been made very clear on more than one occasion; and we simply have to wait on events and see what course the matter may take in the light of the conditions of the war as they develop in the weeks which lie immediately ahead.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is perfectly clear that we will welcome all the children that can be sent?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is no question of that.
May I just say an additional word on how the scheme has worked out so far as the children are concerned. Hon. members will recall that the basis of operation of the scheme was the utilization of the existing welfare agencies in each of the provinces. As a result of conferences held in Ottawa, the plan was developed and homes were carefully inspected by experienced social workers as to their suitability for the reception of the children. That occurred in every province. Here may I pay a very large meed of praise to the provincial governments and to the social welfare agencies under their control which have cooperated in making this scheme, I think, a fine success. These children have been placed all across Canada. It is true that occasionally changes of homes have had to be made; that was inevitable; but I think I may say with confidence that the plan has worked out excellently and that the overwhelming majority of these children are happy and safe; and that is the important thing.
At the commencement of the scheme the British government sent a representative to Canada who was attached to the British high commissioner's office in this city. In the late months of last year and, I believe, the beginning of the present year, this gentleman made a trip across Canada, personally visited a great many of the homes in which children were placed, and met the people who had the direct supervision in the provinces. When he returned he came to my office to express his satisfaction on the whole with the manner in which the plan has worked out. If there are complaints, they have not come to my notice. I think I would have heard something of them if the scheme were not working out on the whole satisfactorily. I have not received by letter a single complaint from any part of

War Appropriation Bill

Canada as to the operation of the scheme, and to the best of my knowledge and belief it is working out in a satisfactory manner. These children are being cared for as though they were the children of the homes in which they are placed. They are receiving proper medical and dental care, adequate clothing for winter weather, and all the educational facilities that the communities in which they reside can provide.
I wish to say here publicly a word of thanks to the supervisory committee that has had under its close and unremitting attention the welfare of these children. As hon. members are aware, Doctor Wallace, president of Queens university, is chairman of this committee; Mr. Logan, president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, is honorary treasurer of the committee.
It may be of interest to the committee to know that quite a considerable sum of money -I cannot at the moment give the precise amount-has been received1, not in response to a public appeal, but by way of voluntary giving on the part of many people throughout Canada and some in the United States who have made contributions to the welfare of the children. These gifts have been applied to such extra expenses as are involved in hospital, medical and dental care where the homes in which the children were placed have not the means themselves to provide these necessaries.
I am glad that the hon. member asked the question, because it has given me the opportunity to state just how the scheme has worked out so far. The amount in the appropriation bill to which my hon. friend referred, is, of course, an estimate. Should the movement be resumed in a large way, all the money may be required. It is put in for that purpose and is about as close a guess as we are able to make at the present time.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES

speechtext:
Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Parks Act for the purpose of withdrawing certain areas of land from the Prince Albert national park as presently constituted, and for establishing new boundaries for the said park as a consequence thereof.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Will the minister explain the object of the resolution? It withdraws certain areas of land from the national park in Prince Albert. What is the area, and what is the purpose of the withdrawal?

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: The total area of the Prince Albert national park at the present time is 1,870 square miles. It is proposed to reduce that by 376 square miles, leaving the park thereafter with an area of 1,494 square miles. The part that will be taken out under this legislation comprises three different blocks, one a comparatively large block which is rather swampy with a certain amount of timber and which, as a matter of fact, should not have been included in the park area in the first instance.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Who is asking for it to be taken out?

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
I will deal with that in a moment. I should say that the areas taken out of the park will revert to the province, but we have reached an understanding with the province that one block of eleven square miles, which is fair Agricultural land, will be added to an Indian reserve near the southeast corner of the park. This additional block of eleven square miles will prove very useful to the Indians on that reserve for development in an agricultural way, and the other small block will probably be opened up to settlement. It lies on the southern boundary of the park.
The reason for this is that it will reduce to some extent the cost of administering the

National Parks-Prince Albert
park. The area has to be patrolled to guard against fire and to protect it against illegal trapping, because trapping is forbidden in the park. After giving the matter considerable thought, the park officials came to the conclusion that the exclusion of these particular areas I have mentioned would reduce the cost of administration and would not detract in any way from the purposes for which the park was created. After I had studied their recommendations, I agreed with them.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Has any survey work been done by the minister's department to find out whether the land to be set aside for agricultural purposes is suitable?

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
No, we have not made any particular surveys of the land. We know the general nature of the land, and we know that similar land is being farmed to-day. My hon. friend is familiar with the Prince Albert district. He knows that north of Saskatchewan river, north and west of Prince Albert, there is fine agricultural country developed as a result of clearing timber off the land, and the information I have is that the two smaller blocks, one of which goes to the Indian reserve, are land of this type. It would be suitable for settlement.

speechtext:
Has this land which
has been classified as agricultural been surveyed by the soil survey department of Saskatchewan? I ask the question because a great deal of land in that part of the province which was thought to be good agricultural land was found after a few years to be leach land and not really suitable for agricultural purposes, although it looked all right. Saskatchewan, has, I believe, done more in soil survey work than any other province, and I was hoping that before any of this land in the north country was opened up for agricultural settlement, the soil survey branch of the university of Saskatchewan would first of all advise as to its suitability. I wonder whether, in throwing open this land out of the park, attention has been given to that matter. In my opinion it is of vital importance, because we are going to have a further relief problem in northern Saskatchewan for the reason that people have settled on land which is not really suitable for agricultural purposes, because it is so badly leached.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
The larger area I spoke
of, lying to the east of the park, is, I am informed, not suitable for agricultural purposes. It is more or less swampy, with some timber. The two smaller areas, one of which goes to the Indian reserve and the other lying at the southern part, have been described to me as fair agricultural land. As regards the part that goes to the reserve, the Saskatchewan government will have nothing to do with its administration. So far as the other part is concerned, that which lies westerly and at the southern boundary of the park, when it will be opened up for settlement and the conditions under which it will be opened up are, of course, matters for the provincial government to deal with. I should think it likely, although I have no knowledge of the subject, that in the light of their experience in the past they would probably have soil surveys made, such as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has referred to, before opening up the land for settlement. That, however, is a matter wholly for the Saskatchewan government to determine. Of course we did not make the provision; indeed, it would have been wholly unwarranted on our part to have made it a condition that they institute a soil survey of this area before they would open it to settlement. We simply arranged with them to take it back. The conditions of settlement are for the Saskatchewan government to determine.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
It seems strange to me why the National Parks Act is being amended for the benefit of these prairie parks, although I am not objecting; but during the last two
National Parks-Prince Albert

or three sessions there was a proposal for an amendment as far as Ontario was concerned. which is almost a similar case, and nothing has been done. Ontario has the smallest area in national parks of any province of the dominion. The proposal was to link up all the government properties from the Trent canal, lake Simcoe, Muskoka, Parry Sound, right through to new Ontario into a grand scheme of national parks, with Muskoka which is very suitable both in summer and winter. What has become of that proposal?

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: f think there was some discussion along the lines my hon. friend has mentioned; indeed, I think he himself advanced that in one of his occasional speeches in the house last session. But there was no proposal of any legislation to amend the parks act or enlarge the parks to take in the various areas he has mentioned. Legislation is necessary in this case because the park boundaries are set under the National Parks Act, and consequently we cannot reduce the area of a park or enlarge it without legislation. The purpose of the legislation in this case I have already stated.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: What has become of the proposal, now six or seven years old, to set up a national park in New Brunswick? About 1934 the former government undertook to establish a national park in that province, and an expert was sent down there to make a survey of the several locations suggested. One, known as the Lepreau area, I think got grade A; the other in Albert county, which some people sought to call the Bennett national park, got grade B. Before that squabble was settled, the change of government came and the Bennett park disappeared. Then a new provincial government came into power in New Brunsw'ick, and I suppose there must have been a dozen-that may be an exaggeration, but at least there were three or four new entries in the race for the location, including one in Victoria-Carleton, and another in Queens county. Perhaps the minister would tell us if that has died a natural death, and who was the executioner?

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
I would not say it has
died either a natural or an unnatural death; I think the idea still has the breath of life in it. An examination was made of several sites, and that data is available in our parks branch. I would draw the attention of my hon. friend to this, that two considerations have to be met before a national park can be established in New Brunswick or anywhere else. The first is that the area selected must be suitable for park purposes. I am sure that

no difficulty will be experienced in meeting that condition in the beautiful province of New Brunswick. Indeed, I have heard it said that the whole province is a park.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
Yes; I
agree with that, but not with the implications of that statement.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: The next considerationand I think this is where the difficulty arose in 1935 or subsequently-is that the area must be conveyed for park purposes without charge to the federal government.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: In other words, the province has to deliver the goods.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
When it comes to establishing a park in New Brunswick, where settlement has existed for many years in practically every part of the province, it means, or at any rate I am so informed, that private properties have to be acquired by the government.
Mr. HANSON	(York-Sunbury):	Some
private properties.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
Some private properties
have to be acquired by the provincial government and transferred free of charge to the federal government. I think that is where the difficulty has arisen. Certainly for two years at least after this government came into office we had a vote of $25,000 a year to carry on preliminary surveys, once the area had been made available to us. So far it has not been made available. I am not criticizing anyone for that; I think very obvious difficulties have arisen. I think it is quite impossible during this time of war to proceed with the establishment of any new parks. I would have great difficulty in convincing my colleague the Minister of Finance that it is desirable to spend money in developing new parks during the war. I have no doubt, however, and I express my own view in the matter quite frankly, that New Brunswick should have a national park, and that when the troubles we are now experiencing have passed away, that province will have a national park.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
I agree
entirely with the last proposition of the minister, that it would be ridiculous to talk about establishing a national park in any province to-day. But I might give him a little piece of information. A park would have been established if his friends in the provincial government could have agreed among themselves, but they absolutely failed to do so.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
I, of course, have no knowledge of that. We deal with these matters, or at any rate we endeavour to, in a coldly realistic way in the departmental administration.

National Parks-Prince Albert

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
I think this discussion is
getting out of order, but if it is in order to discuss the parks of Canada in general I should like to present a claim for Kakabeka falls near Fort William.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
I shall
not pursue the matter any further.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: What is the name of the Indian reserve to which the eleven square miles is being added. Is that the reserve just north of Birch Hill?

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: I am sorry I cannot give my hon. friend the name of the reserve at the moment, but I can describe its location fairly accurately. As I recall now, it is at or near the southeast corner of the park.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: In one of those reserves there is a valuable piece of land on the south side of the Saskatchewan, and I wanted the assurance of the minister that it was not the intention of the department to exchange the eleven square miles which are being added to another portion of the reserve for that very fine piece of land on the south side of the river, which now is included in that reserve.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Oh, no; we would never think of such a thing.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Just what is the saving likely to be? I have not had an}' communications in connection with this park, but it is one of the most valuable tourist centres in Saskatchewan, and we would be greatly disappointed if the beauty of this park should be in any way affected by any such transfer of properties. Could the minister estimate what will be the saving to his department as a result of this transfer?

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
I have no definite figures that I can give my hon. friend as to the saving. Perhaps we might save the expense of a few fire rangers who patrol this area, since, as I have said, it is largely swamp and timber. I can assure my hon. friend that it does not add anything to the beauties of the park; as a matter of fact, it should not have been included in the park area in the first instance. Occasionally we have changed the
boundaries of parks where experience has indicated that it was advisable to do so, and the recommendation for this change came from the officers of the parks branch. As I stated in reply to a question by the leader of the opposition, after I had looked into and studied the matter I agreed with their recommendation, and consequently the resolution is here.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Who is requesting this amendment?

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
I
would suggest that the minister get for us the figures with regard to the administration costs of the park; and, as the hon. member to my left suggested, what is going to be saved. We have all too few parks across Canada now. I understand that this year we are going to spend 8500,000 in advertising to bring tourists to Canada; but if we cut down our parks by so many square miles each year, in another ten or fifteen years we shall not have any parks. We must have some attractions to offer the tourists. The minister says these are swamp lands, but I think that is the very part that should be retained, because that is the part of the park where the deer and wild animals feed during the winter.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: I think I would be in a position to give the hon. gentleman the information he has requested with regard to savings when the estimates of the parks branch are before the committee at a later stage. Let me relieve his apprehension at once as to the effect of this transfer on the general park system of Canada. I agree that it is desirable to have these national playgrounds, and for quite a number of years now, successive dominion governments have spent considerable sums of money in developing our parks. Since the present government came into office at the end of 1935, two new parks have been developed or are in process of development, one the Cape Breton Highlands park in Nova Scotia-[DOT]

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
Which
will be one of the best in Canada in time.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
-which is a matter of very great pride to my colleague the minister of naval services, and also a park in Prince Edward Island. If conditions had remained normal; if our revenues had been fairly buoyant and we could have afforded it, I think it would have been the policy of the government to increase the number of these national parks throughout Canada. I am a thorough believer in the national park system.
National Parks-Prince Albert

Perhaps my hon. friend did not hear me, or he may not have been in the chamber when I stated earlier that all we are doing in this instance is reducing the area of the Prince Albert national park from 1,870 square miles to 1,494 square miles. In making this reduction we are not detracting in any degree whatever from the essential features of the park. We still have a very large area, and we have to keep a balance in these things. For instance, a park of 1,500 square miles requires a great deal of patrolling, and necessitates the expenditure of money for protection against fires and so on. We are turning back to the province an area of swamp and forest land. The province will assume the responsibility of protecting that area against fire, and our expenditures will be reduced correspondingly. How much they will be reduced, I cannot say at the moment.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: When that land is turned back, will the province keep it in its present condition?

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: That is their business.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: I do not know. I should think that would be up to this government. I was in the house: I have the figures the minister gave, but I should like to know if the province will keep that land in its present condition. Some restriction should be imposed.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: No; we could not do that; it would be quite impossible. I think my hon. friend will realize that if he gives the matter a moment's thought. This land reverts to the province and becomes part of the public domain of the province, which administers it just as it administers the rest of its public domain. I have been advised that there is a certain amount of timber on this part, I do not know how much, which will be transferred back to the province. I have no doubt that they will look after it just as effectively as we would be able to look after it, and perhaps even more so, because they have the timber areas adjoining.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: What I was afraid of was that the province might get in there and make a slash through this timber, which would be a detriment to the park. Some restriction should be put on, so that they would have to keep it in good shape.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
We cannot put on any restrictions when we return the land to the province, but I do not think my hon. friend's concern in that regard is very sound. I have no doubt that the province will look after this area, and this transfer will not affect the remainder of the park in any event.
fMr. Crerar.]

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: There is some value to the point just made by the hon. member for Peterborough West. There is the further point that very often, when areas are thrown open for farm settlement, the fire hazard increases. I am not familiar with this portion of the park, but I think some precaution should be taken to see that the park forest should not be endangered by land settlement which might be carried out by the provincial government.

subtopic: PEINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
I do not think there is any foundation for that fear, either. As a matter of fact, settlement does adjoin the park now over a considerable length of its boundaries, and our experience has been that there is very little danger of fire originating on farms adjoining the park. It is of interest to note that it is estimated that 80 per cent of the forest fires in Canada are what are described as man-made fires. The remaining 20 per cent may be due to natural causes, such as lightning. The higher percentage would be due to carelessness on the part of campers and people travelling through the forests. That is what we have to guard against within the park boundaries. Someone smoking a cigarette may be driving along a road in an automobile. When the cigarette is half consumed it may be thrown out of the window of the car, and start a fire which may do a great deal of damage. That is the sort of thing we have to guard against in patrolling these park areas. I might say there is a road which passes through this swampy timbered area which we are returning to the province. It passes through the park down to Montreal lake to get into water courses which go away back into the Lac la Ronge country.
