maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD

speechtext:
Hon. C. D. HOWE (for the Minister of Transport) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act, 1937, changing the period for the fixation of rates for the current year, as defined in the act, and extending the initial period during which a subsidy may be payable to Trans-Canada Air Lines.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Vien in the chair.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
Would the minister make an explanation now, or shall we ask questions later on?

Trans-Canada Air Lines

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
I should be glad to explain. The bill to be based on this resolution has the effect of further extending the date after which the rates for the carriage of mail by Trans-Canada Air Lines will be fixed automatically by the financial results of the preceding year. Our difficulty in applying the automatic feature is that the traffic is growing very rapidly on Trans-Canada Air Lines, and the mileage operated is growing to meet the requirements of the traffic.
In the year ended December 31, 1940, about 5,000,000 miles were operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines, and the plans for the fiscal year 1941-42 call for the operation of well over 7,500,000 miles, or more than 50 per cent increase in the mileage flown. Of course the greater mileage and the increasing traffic increase the operating profits of the company. Based on the operating results of last year, the automatic feature of the bill would fix a rate of fifty-three cents a mile for the mail rate for 1940-41. We feel, however, that in view of the increased mileage and the steady increase in business on the line we can do rather better than that for the post office, and the objective will be to fix a rate of not fifty-three cents a mile but forty cents a mile, as the basic mail rate, which is a reduction of course from sixty cents a mile to forty cents.
Last year the earnings of the air lines, after all write-offs and interest on investment, was something over $500,000. This year it is anticipated that the earnings from air mail based on the increased mileage and the 40cent rate will be S3,153,000. The passenger revenue will be $2,170,000. Miscellaneous revenue, comprised chiefly of express, will amount to $250,000, giving a total gross revenue of $5,573,500. Operating expenses are anticipated to be $5,315,477, giving an operating income of $258,032, less interest on capital, and other income charges, of $197,500. That leaves us with an estimated surplus of $60,523.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
After
depreciation?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Yes; depreciation is an operating charge.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
What is it
figured at?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
At 25 per cent of the value of the aeroplanes, engines and flying equipment; I believe the rate is 10 per cent on the buildings. I might say that throughout the period of the operation of Trans-Canada Air Lines we have had a steady increase in the poundage of mail carried, subject to seasonal variations. Over an average period the increase in the amount of mail carried
has been at the rate of 4 per cent per month, a very steady increase. Anticipating that this increase will continue throughout the fiscal year 1941-42, we have reached the point where the post office will almost break even on revenue as against expenditure, counting four cents of the six cents charged for air mail as revenue to the air mail, and two cents as the cost to the post office for the collection and distribution of the mail. A very slight increase in mail beyond the normal increase will balance the books, and we anticipate that in the following fiscal year the post office will make a profit on the sale of air mail stamps.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: On the basis of forty cents?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
Yes. We have also brought the cost of carrying air mail down to about the level that is current in the United States. I may say that this is something of a freak, because our equipment costs us about 50 per cent more than similar equipment in the United States, since we pay duty, sales tax and all other charges on the equipment when we bring it into Canada. Also we are charged higher rates for gasoline than are paid by air lines in the United States.
For purposes of comparison, the mail rate on the Trans-Continental and Western Air Line, from New York to Los Angeles, via Chicago, is forty cents a mile; on the Canadian Colonial Airways, from New York to Montreal, forty cents per mile; on Northeast Airlines, from Boston to Caribou, Maine, thirty-six cents per mile; and on Northwestern Airways, Minneapolis to Winnipeg, thirty-seven cents per mile. Therefore, while passing through the development period, in the brief time Trans-Canada has been in operation we have succeeded in getting the mail rate down to a comparable basis with similar services in the United States. We have succeeded in building up a volume of mail much more quickly than had ever been anticipated. When we started the line we anticipated that five years must elapse before the post office could break even on its operations, but we are on the point of achieving that in about three years' operation, and we shall have at the end of the year a service that, I think, will be adequate for the business of Canada. Of course, this will always be an expanding service, but at the end of this expansion the changes will be more normal and the automatic feature of the act will then operate quite properly.
This bill makes one other change in the situation. The fiscal year of Trans-Canada Air Lines is the calendar year, and formerly it was provided that any change in rates would take place on January 1, but there were operating difficulties in getting the data to fix the new
Trans-Canada Air Lines

rate on January 1. It usually takes from one month to six weeks to close the books of Trans-Canada, and there was also the difficulty of the post office budgeting for a fiscal year when there might be a change in the rate in the last three months of the fiscal year. Therefore, the bill provides that hereafter the rate established under the automatic feature for the carriage of mail shall extend from March 31 in one year to March 31 in the following year.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: What the minister has told us of this bill and the effect of last year's bill would seem to indicate that the automatic rate fixing structure in the statute as originally passed was entirely out of line. Is that about the effect of it?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: It is out of line when there is a very rapid expansion of the mileage, but there will come a time, and it is coming I think after this year, when I do not think we shall have to ask parliament for such extensions because the mileage will be reasonably stabilized. There will be the matter perhaps of an extra trip on a given route or a short route may be added to the mileage, but that will not seriously affect the automatic feature. A fifty per cent addition such as we anticipate this year would, of course, increase the earnings to a point where the automatic feature would not be fair to the post office.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is a matter for congratulation that Canada has made such headway and achieved this fair amount of success in the operation of Trans-Canada Air Lines. A good deal of that success, as the minister probably admitted in his statement to-night, has been due to the fact that so far as financing is concerned the post office has helped out very considerably.
The minister was good enough to give a few of the rates that apply on certain runs in the United States. The rates he quoted were in the neighbourhood of forty cents a mile, with one as low as thirty-six cents. Perhaps, before we pass this bill, the minister, who no doubt has the information before him, will tell the committee if there are rates in force in the United States as low as nineteen cents a mile.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: They are not comparable rates.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
Rates
caused by competition, perhaps.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
Take, for
instance, the average rate for the carrying of mail in the United States. I would not want the impression left upon the committee that we were carrying our mails at a lower 
cost than that which obtains in the United States. As I say, I am not complaining. I think it is a matter for congratulation that the Postmaster General was able to get this legislation before the house and get the rate down from the very high rate of sixty cents. The observation I made on a previous occasion I repeat now, that when the balance sheet was struck, with a rate of sixty cents; when depreciation charges were provided for, and quite substantial depreciation charges, in some instances as high as twenty-five per cent, and when interest charges were taken care of, the statement was made that they had earned big money, and I notice that the minister in his statement said, "Our earnings will be such and such". Quite so, so far as bookkeeping earnings are concerned. But is it real earnings so far as the consolidated balance sheet of the Dominion of Canada is concerned? The word "subsidy" has been used, and I think it would apply to a degree.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
It is quite an improper use of
the word "subsidy."

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Very well, we will reserve our opinion with regard to that. It certainly is not now a subsidy to the same degree as obtained previously. Previous balance sheets showed as much as $2 revenue received from the post office till as against SI for the carriage of passengers. The post office will contribute $3,153,000 and the passenger service, $2,170,000, with a few miscellaneous services which do not affect the picture. I look forward to the day when passenger and other revenues will be sufficient to equalize at least the post office-I shall have to find a new word for subsidy-contract, we will call it. I am gratified to note that there has been a continual increase in the amount of business, an increase of four per cent on the average, but I think that is not enough.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Four per cent a month.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
That is forty-eight per cent a year. That is a good record. But we shall not be able to keep that up beyond a few years.
As to passenger travel, we have had a minimum of accidents, and I say to the minister that those of us who feel disposed to look into the work of the department and offer constructive criticism must not be charged with being parties to wanting to demoralize the service, as it were, or not giving it all the attention required, with the result that now and then there may be accidents. Gasoline costs are higher, and then there are sales tax and all these other charges to be taken care of. But more and more attention should, I believe, be given by Canadians to the service given

Trans-Canada Air Lines
by Trans-Canada Air Lines. It is a good way to travel, and I should like to see more members of the Canadian House of Commons
using this service.
I saw a skit in a Toronto newspaper of Friday, March 14, which read:
A member of a reserve unit writes, re transportation for the soldiers:
"If there is room on the train for big fat politicians like Joseph Harris, there should be room for people like these boys."
That will be found-I hope the press is listening-in the issue of Friday last.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
What
paper?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: The Toronto Telegram. I am not complaining at all, because every knock is a boost, as we all know, otherwise I probably could not have answered the roll call for two decades.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: They have said worse things than that about some of us.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: I merely wanted to point out the irony of that suggestion because, in order to be here after completing a day's work in Toronto, I was privileged to ride to Ottawa by plane, and pay my fare. And this is the newspaper report I find when I get here.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: That would not be the first mistake which that paper has made.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: I suggest to the government that it might cancel all these passes. I say to my friends the press that this is the sixth time I have urged in the House of Commons the cancellation of all passes, so that the railways would come that much nearer to balancing their budget; yet I got a telephone call on Monday last from Trans-Canada Air Lines to my office, asking me if I would pay my fare or whether I was travelling on a pass.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: My hon. friend never was asked that. He is mistaken. There is a policy under which S300 is paid and put in a credit and charged to the passenger's account. Nobody travels with a pass on the Trans-Canada.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: The question asked was, was I travelling on a pass or was I paying my fare. I am not complaining about the question. They have a right to ask it because, as I understand it, those who travel on passes on the Trans-Canada Air Lines have to take second place to those who pay their fares.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: I understand there are no passes.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: The minister can correct me if I am wrong. I understand that, if there is a spare seat, a person who rides free can have it. If all the seats are taken by paying passengers, those who travel on passes have to wait. That is quite a proper provision, but I would go further and cancel all passes on the Trans-Canada Air Lines. That is only by the way; it gave me an opportunity to reply to a suggestion which I noticed with some pleasure in the press.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: The cost would not be so light to British Columbia as it is to Toronto.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Quite; and following up the point the hon. member has raised, as far as railway and aeroplane passes are concerned this house should deal with the matter in a businesslike way, the same as any industry, and pay a voucher, in the case of any hon. member travelling on government business, whether he comes from the Yukon or Halifax. Then we would be all on a parity. It would, however, stop a lot of joy-rides.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Cut them all out.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
Yes, when an institution is not making money, and Canada has to foot the bill.
I should like the minister to explain what effect will the changing of the date have. What rate applies? Does sixty cents apply to the' end of December, and forty cents from then on, or does sixty cents carry through until the end of March?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Answering the question of my hon. friend, the sixty cent rate carries through to the 31st of March, and the forty cent rate obtains for the fiscal year, April to April.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
Just before this resolution is passed, as I assume it will be, I rise to pay to the minister who introduced it what I believe is a well-earned tribute for his development and administration of this difficult service. I shall spend only a moment on it. I know something of the story. It fell to the lot of our minister to take on this task while he was Minister of Transport, administering the department of railways, the department of marine, and what is sometimes described as that other department, radio. He was in competition with four east and west air lines in the United States, nearly all of which had been established for ten or eleven years, tapping a business, both postal and passenger, with which our sparsely populated country furnishes no parallel whatever. In the administrative personnel that he selected and in the operating personnel that

Trans-Canada Air Lines

he selected, barring one misfortune of recent date which appears to have been one of those accidents for which no one could be held responsible, the administration of this service and the place it now occupies in the east and west traffic of this continent are remarkable. There is one man more than any other who is responsible for its success, and that is our minister who has had the responsibility for the work.
In addition to setting up the system, he has had to negotiate with the authorities at Washington regarding many intricate and difficult problems of air service between our country and the republic to the south. I had personally an opportunity of learning the respect in which the board at Washington hold our minister, and the success he has had in these delicate and difficult negotiations. I believe that I am speaking for almost every hon. member in taking this opportunity to pay a measure of tribute to him for the big job he has done.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
I cannot
pay an equal tribute to the minister-I see him blushing over there at the words of encomium from his follower-but I will take it for granted that everything said is correct and endorse what has been done. There is, however, one criticism about this service in the east.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Don't spoil it!

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
Well, I
have a duty to perform. I shall do it as quickly as possible.
The Saint John Telegraph-Journal, which is the leading morning newspaper in New Brunswick, published on March 18 an editorial under the caption, "Our Unsatisfactory Air Service." I had no idea that this matter would come up to-night, but I am going to read this to the minister and then leave it with him, in the hope that he will draw it to the attention of the officials of Trans-Canada and see if something can be done.
It is not based on the fact that the terminus has been changed from Moncton to Halifax. Our friends, I think, put over rather a fast one on the hon. member for Westmorland. I suppose that while he slept, they were working. Personally I believe it will do no harm to anyone to have the terminus at Halifax; in fact, I regard it as a logical growth of the system. It may hurt the pride of Moncton a little bit to feel that they are no longer the eastern terminus of Trans-Canada, but they are going to be served by Trans-Canada as well as and perhaps better than they have been in the past.

This is the voice of Saint John, and of course some of us must pay attention to it. Here is the complaint:
Changes in the Trans-Canada airways service east of Montreal, under which the large passenger liners which hitherto stopped at Moncton will soon be continuing on to Halifax, will leave the large port city of Saint John and New Brunswick's capita.! city of Fredericton in the same unsatisfactory position as they have been since the T.C.A. lines were extended to this province. Prior to their advent there was a service between Saint John and Halifax which is not now operating. The plan just announced at Ottawa is to the effect that early in April the Montreal to Moncton plane, after stopping at Moncton, will continue on to Halifax, thus doing away with the transfer at Moncton to a smaller plane. The return trip from Halifax will also be via Moncton. So far as the situation as regards other important places in New Brunswick is concerned, it remains exactly as it was-practically no air service. Fredericton has no connections at all, and Saint John is on the end of a so-called feeder line which makes connections at Moncton to and from Montreal, but no connections with Halifax. Air mail from Saint John to Halifax is flown to Moncton in the afternoon, but it arrives too late to connect with the Halifax plane, and must go on from there by train.
That seems to me a cause of complaint which could perhaps be easily remedied if the Postmaster General, who, I know, is alert in the discharge of the duties of his office, would give ear to that complaint and have that plane started a little earlier in order to have it make connection with the Halifax plane. If that were done, that complaint would be done away with.
Likewise, mail from Halifax is brought by train to connect with the aeroplane for Saint John.
I do not understand why that is. I should think that the mail would come up by plane and be transferred there. There ought to be some cooperation with the feeder system.
The same situation exists with regard to passengers. If a person wants to fly from Saint John to Halifax, he is obliged to remain overnight and until early the next afternoon in Moncton, and adopt the same procedure on the return trip. In other words, it consumes two full days to make the return trip.
I have not checked on that, but I think it is true. Of course that is an impossible situation with regard to aeroplane travel between the two Atlantic cities. This, then, is the complaint of the newspaper:
It is about time that some serious consideration was given to this thoroughly unsatisfactory situation. Here are the two principal cities on the eastern seaboard, between which there is an increasing commercial traffic, virtually without air connection, and the capital of this province entirely omitted from the plan.
Well, in Fredericton we are used to that. Unfortunately, we have never been on the main line; nevertheless we are very happy

Trans-Canada Air Lines
indeed, and some day perhaps we shall get aeroplane connection. I have no high hopes in the immediate future, but I will revert in a moment to a situation which may help to remedy that. The article goes on:
Many efforts have been made to remedy this deficiency but all to no avail. Now that something is being done to improve the service between Montreal and Halifax, the matter of a service between Saint John and Halifax and connections with Fredericton deserves immediate consideration.
I think the situation between Saint John and Halifax ought to be remedied within a reasonably short space of time. I cannot see very much hope for air connection with Fredericton. I do not believe the traffic presently offering would pay for a feeder service. It may be that in time it will be developed, but I have had some conversation with the minister with regard to the development of the Blissville air field. That was established by the late government as an emergency landing field. It is on the beam between Moncton and Montreal. It is only thirty-five miles from Fredericton and about the same distance from Saint John. I hope that the government will do something this year, and I entertain high hopes in that regard from what the minister has said about developing that field, so that planes can land there with a much greater degree of safety than at the present time. There are no runways. The field has been cleared and put into shape and it ought to be extended somewhat, and some runways built. I hope the minister will give consideration to having Blissville established as a permanent port of call, or at least as a flag station. Perhaps that is a fair thing to ask for at the start. If business is offering between Montreal and Moncton, then I hope he will consider having the Blissville air field established as a port of call if, as and when it is required. That would be, as far as I know, the only solution of the problem of aeroplane service as between Moncton and Halifax on the one hand and Montreal on the other, in respect of Fredericton at least.
I do not think the cost of building an air port at Blissville would be very great, and of course it would be a great convenience to a great many people, who could utilize it to get to Montreal quickly by evening plane. I believe that one reason why it has not been pressed for before is that we have an excellent train service from western New Brunswick to Montreal. You leave in the evening and are in Montreal the next morning. Being now at the advanced age of sixty-two, and not being air-minded, I find that method of transportation quite good enough for myself. I have never thought I had any business up there; my wife tells me the same thing, and 14873-111}	'
I am not proposing this on my own account. I am quite content to travel in the good old-fashioned way, but I seriously suggest to the minister that he give some consideration immediately, if he will, to this complaint about lack of connection for both air mail and aeroplane passenger service between Saint John and Halifax.
There was an airways company which operated a plane service on a triangular basis covering Moncton, Halifax and Saint John. I would suppose that company could not continue. I believe they do the Island work, with certain flights to the Magdalen islands and they are open for charter; but that service will not continue, at least not without some kind of mail subsidy, and I assume, from the arrangements made with Trans-Canada, that this is out of the question now so far as Saint John and Halifax are concerned.
I do not think it is asking too much to have a decent feeder service between Saint John and Moncton so as to take advantage of their planes. I would ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who has the aeroplane situation under his guidance, and the Postmaster General to put their heads together and find a solution of this problem. If they do not, they will hear more about it at a later date.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
There is one
further question I wish to ask, for the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) of the Postmaster General. At Malton there are, to my knowledge, no post office facilities, with the result that air mail going from Ottawa or Montreal to Toronto goes to Malton, and from Malton it takes it an hour to get to the general post office where it is sorted for dispatch to its destination. The net result is that it is almost as quick to send mail in the ordinary way from Montreal to Toronto or from Ottawa to Toronto as against the air mail facilities. It would be of advantage if some post office arrangement were made at Malton, or air mail directed there so that, if picked up there, there would be a considerable saving of time and more of the mail service between those points would be used.
Perhaps the minister in charge of this matter would be kind enough to let the Postmaster General put on record the position, and if he feels so disposed, the other question also with regard to the rates obtaining in the United States other than those the minister put on record. The statute of 1937 definitely says that this rate is a matter of negotiation between the Postmaster General and the minister of the department administering the Trans-Canada Air Lines. We have the Trans-Canada Air Lines point of view on record with regard to these negotiations. Would the

Trans-Canada Air Linen
Postmaster General put his point of view on record, and how he came to agree to the 40cent rate? I realize that it is lower than the fifty-three cents which might have been payable, but at the same time I can visualize that he had some difficulty in reducing a rate from sixty to forty cents, and I think that ought to be put on record.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
I shall be glad to discuss the question of putting postal employees at Malton with the official in charge of air mail, and also with the hon. member.
Regarding the second matter, that of the attitude of the post office towards this rate, I may say that we are well satisfied with the arrangement that we have been able to make with Trans-Canada Air Lines. The minister in charge has been very cooperative, has given us every possible assistance. We sat down with officials of each department and worked out what we thought was a fair rate.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
And saved a
million dollars for your department.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: That was one idea, I may tell my hon. friend. So far as the post office is concerned, naturally we would be glad to have the rate reduced still further, but I think he will agree that Trans-Canada has made an excellent showing and that the post office has made a pretty good bargain in getting a reduction from sixty cents to forty cents in one year.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
It all
depends on whether sixty cents was too high before.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Still, it is a substantial reduction. If we could be so fortunate as to reduce some of our debts and taxation in the same measure, it would be very satisfactory.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
What is the
grand average for the United States?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: It depends what lines you take. I think that is a matter for the Minister of Munitions and Supply to deal with. I do not want to encroach on his department.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: It is fair to state that a number of these rates in the United States are established by competition between air lines which want the distinction of carrying the United States mails. They seem to think there is something in that. I understand that some rates from New York south are as low as nineteen cents.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
Would the minister
endeavour to settle a doubt which arises in my mind, and I am sure in the minds of many, in connection with the projected increase in flying miles from 5,000,000 to 7,500,000, an

increase of 50 per cent. That seems almost incredible in time of war, and surely must interfere with our war effort. I noticed in a recent United States paper that the United States government through its proper agency was limiting the expansion of the airways in that country to a very modest degree. The air line companies were allowed to purchase only sufficient planes to replace those wearing out in the service and add in a very meagre way. Would the minister explain why it is necessary that the Trans-Canada should expand fifty per cent in this year 1941 when we know that planes are so badly needed, particularly the large bomber type which is used in the Trans-Canada service, especially in view of the fact that these planes must be purchased in the United States and that I believe in the last twelve or fourteen months we have used nearly a million dollars of United States exchange in the purchase of these planes.
If there is a demand for aeroplane transportation in war business, either passenger or mail, surely we can use the existing facilities for the very necessary purpose of expediting the war effort and raise the mail rate from six cents to twelve cents, or whatever rate might be feasible, and also raise passenger fares which at present are not very much higher than railway fares. It would appear that Trans-Canada Air Lines are making severe competition for the railways as to passengers and for the post office as to ordinary letter mail, when the air mail postage rate is only six cents as against three cents. If it is so necessary that war business be carried by air, surely we could, by raising the rates, eliminate much unnecessary other business in these trying times.
Another question, which is perhaps slightly divorced from those I have mentioned, is this: We all feel that the Minister of Munitions and Supply, under whose aegis the Trans-Canada Air Lines come, is a much overburdened man. He was good enough to tell me privately why it was that Trans-Canada Air Lines continued under his jurisdiction. I am sorry to say, however, that his statement did not sufficiently impress itself upon my memory, although I think I understood it at the time. It would be of interest if he would explain why it is that he as one of the busiest members of the cabinet still keeps Trans-Canada Air Lines under his jurisdiction.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend's first question was whether the contemplated expansion in mileage would interfere with the war effort. I would say that at least fifty per cent of our business is in connection with those travelling up and down the country on war business. It is a very great convenience for people to be able to get in a plane in the

Trans-Canada Air Lines
morning, come to Ottawa, do their business and be back home the same evening, as many do. It is a great convenience to be able to telephone a man in Vancouver and have him in Ottawa next morning to discuss the business we have in hand.
We bought six planes this year, but they were bought out of the depreciation fund of the Trans-Canada Air Lines. No new capital was involved. Of course the purpose of a depreciation fund is to make sure that we do not end a certain period with no equipment. The purpose of the fund is to keep the equipment up to a standard.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: But you bought six new planes; you could not keep your full number of old ones and add six new ones out of depreciation.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Yes; the age of the old ones was getting on, and as we take them out of service we add new planes. We had at one time a fleet of fifteen planes; we lost one in an unfortunate accident; we have fourteen old planes and six new ones. The old planes are about three years old; they have a theoretical life of four years, and we have six of a larger and more expensive type bought to replace those planes. Of course it is desirable not to have all your planes bought the same year but to stagger them so that some end their theoretical life each year. However, as I say we have not changed the capital of Trans-Canada Air Lines. The capital invested is $3,250,000, and it is not anticipated that additional capital will be required at any future stage.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
We cannot purchase
these planes for use against the enemy and at the same time use the planes in Canada.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend
we are purchasing a good many planes both for training and for use against the enemy.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
All we can get, I should
suggest.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: What was the next question?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
The minister's answers
do not quite satisfy me. I feel, as I am sure we all do, that every available plane should be used overseas. There has been a shortage of planes; we all know that production in this country has not been all that we hoped for, and here we are using what I might term the very lifeblood of the country for a purely domestic service. At the same time we are using United States funds for the purchase of these planes, which means that these funds are not available for the purchase of planes or other war equipment which could be used in the first line of defence across the ocean. For that reason I think we should go as
easily as possible in the expansion of this service during this extremely critical period. I know that Trans-Canada Air Lines has had a splendid record, but from the experience of many who have used it I feel that they could have travelled by train just as easily. The great centres of industry are in Quebec and Ontario. If a man from Toronto uses a plane, it merely means that he sleeps at home rather than on the train, so there would be no very great loss of time if he travelled by train. The same thing applies to a man living in Montreal. It is true that this service is a great convenience to anyone going to the Pacific coast; but there, as we have heard so often in this house, there is not a great deal of war industry. For these reasons I feel that this committee should seriously consider this great expansion of Trans-Canada Air Lines at this time.
That was one of the points I raised. I also suggested that if it should be considered necessary to confine traffic on the air line to the war effort, as it were, the rates should be increased so that unnecessary commercial and pleasure traffic could be eliminated and the available space left for those people who really have a vital need to use these planes. That was my second point. The third question was why the minister should keep this department under his jurisdiction together with the very important work he is doing in connection with munitions and supply.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
It is necessary to maintain
transportation facilities in this country even though we are fighting a war. We are buying box cars, passenger cars and rolling stock all the time. We are buying equipment to haul tourists to Banff and Lake Louise from points in the United States, and we are purchasing aeroplanes so that we may bring tourists from New York to Toronto and open up new routes of that kind. We must maintain our communications in this country. If they are necessaiy in peace time they are even more necessary in war time; and I think the capital cost of these planes in United States funds will be only a small fraction of the United States funds which will be brought into Canada by the run between Toronto and New York.
As for rates, the act requires that the rates charged in Canada shall be competitive with the rates in the United States. As a matter of fact, they are exactly the same, both for mail and for passenger traffic, except that we collect in Canadian funds and across the line they collect in United States funds. It would be quite impossible, of course, to have a rate for air mail in Canada different from the rate for air mail in the United States,
Trans-Canada Air Lines

because the two are readily interchangeable. That would only make more confusion. Similarly, in my opinion, the passenger traffic should be competitive.
As to why I kept the department under my jurisdiction, I did it as a matter of convenience. I was Minister of Transport at the same time that I was responsible for the war supply board. A considerable part of the work at that time had to do with the construction of a number of air fields across Canada; that is still an important part of the work. In the Department of Transport we had developed a large, highly trained staff familiar with the work of locating, designing and supervising the construction of airports. When I left the Department of Transport I thought it would be a very great convenience if I could retain the use of that staff. There was also the fact that the radio control at military airports is the same as the radio control at civil airports; and there again we had a staff well trained in the installation and operation of the controls. It was a convenience to have that staff associated with the department that was building the military controls. The department of air services is a unit; the same technicians serve the radio department, the meteorological department and the air regulations department. In taking one branch of that service, it is practically necessary to keep the three together. As a matter of fact, the meteorological work is very closely associated with the work of military airports, in that we have a man from the weather bureau at each military airport, and we also have teletype communication between the central weather service and the military airports. This department was taken over as a matter of convenience. If I do not object to the strain, and if hon. members do not object to the service the branch is giving, frankly I do not think it is anyone's affair very much, except the government's as to who has the department.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Before the minister leaves that, would he not say a word of encouragement about the matter I brought up, namely, the service between Saint John and Halifax, both air mail and air passenger.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
Yes, I should say something about that. We have had difficulty in working out a satisfactory service to the maritimes, but gradually we have been able to iron out those difficulties. The first difficulty we had was that with only one trip to Moncton it was hard to satisfy both the passenger service and the air mail service. Obviously the best mail service to the maritimes should involve a late evening departure from Montreal, a departure after six o'clock from Toronto and an early morning arrival in Moncton, so that

the mail could be landed in the three large maritime cities in time for the first delivery. That would suit the mail very well, and we tried that service, but we found that the passengers did not care to travel at night. Therefore we took the alternative of satisfying the passengers. WTe have now a morning departure from Toronto, a departure before noon from Montreal and an arrival in Moncton which brings the mail to the maritime cities too late for distribution the same day. That is not satisfactory from a mail point of view, although it seems to be satisfactory from the passenger point of view. This year, however, traffic has developed to such a point as to warrant both services, and this year I think we shall be able to satisfy both the mail and the passenger requirements.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: That is on the through service?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Yes. We have had difficulty with the short run from Moncton to Saint John. It is a difficult run. It is too short to warrant the exclusive use of an aeroplane, and it has been worked in on other services. I will admit at once that it is not at all satisfactory to the city of Saint John, but I would state also that when the Moncton airport can be put in condition, a much more satisfactory service to Saint John and Fredericton will be possible.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Does the minister mean the Blissville airport?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: Yes. I would, however, point out to my hon. friend that to make a first-class field out of Blissville is a serious job. It is not difficult to make a runway in one direction, but it is difficult to get a runway of the proper length in the other direction. We are studying the matter.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
I had
somewhat different information from that of the engineer.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
No; parallel to the track it is not difficult to extend the runway, and that is the runway which would be most used. But to get across the runway 4,000 feet is very difficult, because you run back into a heavy excavation. I am hopeful that we shall be able to satisfy Trans-Canada with the improvements we can make this year, and get a stop there by autumn. If we can, it will improve the situation materially. But we have to let Trans-Canada be the judge as to whether or not they would be justified in making the stop. We hope to be able to satisfy them with the Blissville field.
Our difficulty in getting into Halifax was the conflict with the air force operational authorities. Some strenuous objection was

Trans-Canada Air Lines
made to our coming into their area of operations; but experience has shown that the two services do not seriously conflict. We have another problem in the maritimes, namely, the service to Sydney. Of all the maritime cities, probably air service would be more beneficial to Sydney than to any other, because it is a long rail trip from Moncton.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: That is quite right.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: We are studying that service, and we hope that before the summer is far advanced, we shall have a service from Moncton not only to Prince Edward Island cities but also to Sydney. These are problems we are working hard to meet. Of course it has taken a few years to build these air lines, and they are not perfect yet. But I can assure my hon. friend that we appreciate the problems of the maritimes and appreciate that our service is far from perfect at the moment. We will, however, improve it as rapidly as funds will permit.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the work of the Trans-Canada Air Lines must be considered from the commercial aspect, whether it be for the carrying of passengers or mail. This is a luxury service. When we survey the figures for last year of $3,150,000 from the post office and $2,170,000 from passenger service, we see at once that, ever since the air service 'has been given, the Toronto post office has not been receiving the ordinary postal service it used to receive. All this arises as a result of giving this luxury air service.
After all is said and done, the average business man, the retail grocer, or the wholesaler, or the householder, is interested in the main function of the Toronto post office. I have had dozens of complaints since Trans-Canada Air Lines began operations, all to the effect that the other local services are being starved so that this luxury service may be given. For instance, Toronto, with its eight million postal receipts, should have one-cent drop letters, but we do not have that privilege. Then, labour conditions in the post office service at Toronto are deplorable, and should be changed and bettered. In fact, I have fifteen or twenty letters I shall show the minister which would indicate that the department has set up, in effect, a sweatshop, all as a result of starving the original post office services to carry out the functions of this luxury service, and use the receipts of the Toronto post office for outside purposes.
In the residential districts letters are not received until the first mail delivery at eleven o'clock or eleven-thirty in the morning. In the business district the department is not
giving the service it used to give. Whether it be the Trans-Canada Air Lines luxury service, or some other part of the service, the Post Office Department is a public utility, and it should give an up-to-date and efficient service equal to that given by the Bell Telephone Company, the Consumers Gas Company, or any other public utility. The Post Office Department should not live in the past. It should give us the proper service and permit its employees to work under reasonable conditions of labour, as to hours, holidays, overtime and work conditions. In fact, I would ask the Minister of Labour to look into labour conditions in the Toronto post office district I have indicated. They are deplorable, and there should be an inquiry into them. The men have to work long hours, and usually have to work at least part time for holidays. Then they work shifts, part at night and part in the day time. Some work at night all the year round, and have been doing that for several years. The schedules should be revised'.
I contend that the Toronto post office service has been starved for outside places. We cannot get the service because, by bookkeeping or otherwise, the revenues are diverted to another account known as the luxury service elsewhere. The heads and staff are excellent. I am not here to complain about air service; it is a splendid service, and I believe it will be better in the future. But I do wish that the money might be utilized so that the post office might give better work conditions and wages, and a better service to the residential and business areas in Toronto, so that we might have drop letters, and services along many other lines.
In my opinion, this Trans-Canada air service is a public utility, and should be run from the commercial aspect. The rates should meet all maintenance and operational charges, and if they are not doing that, some other older branches of the service are going to be starved, and labour conditions are not going to be what they should be.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: First of all, I should like to ask the hon. member for Rosedale if I understood him correctly: Did he advocate an increase in the air mail rate from six cents to twelve cents?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
I suggested that if Trans-Canada Air Lines was necessary for the carrying on of our war effort in Canada, it might be possible to eliminate some of the surplus passengers and mail now being carried by Trans-Canada Air Lines, and that this might be done by raising the rate. That is the ordinary way in which we eliminate all unnecessary things, and maintain those which
Trans-Canada Air Lines

are essential. Passengers could pay more, because the rates on Trans-Canada both for mail and for passengers are extremely low. The mail rate competes with the rate on ordinary mail, being only six cents as against three cents and the rates on railway trains are almost as high as they are on Trans-Canada. I suggest that if we must confine the operations of Trans-Canada Air Lines to important war services, this can be done by raising the rates.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
I suggest to the hon. member that he is accurate in one statement, namely, that he would eliminate air mail, or a great part of it. He would, however, add another problem; he would add a tremendous deficit to the Post Office Department. I might say that I should like to do something toward making it a paying department, rather than one which is losing money. I believe, if the hon. member would reconsider his suggestion, he would see at once that it is not one which would help the revenues of the department. Certainly it would not be of any great assistance in increasing the volume of business. It is the volume of business which makes it possible for Trans-Canada to operate. I hope he is not seriously suggesting that we should stop our air mail service at this time. If the policy of dismemberment which once took place were continued, I might say that we would not have the air fields available in Canada to-day, air fields which are available because of construction by Trans-Canada Air Lines. Those air fields are available for purposes of training, and for the defence of the nation. I believe the hon. member, in the interests of both air mail and defence, would do well to reconsider his suggestion, because it is the financing of this volume of business which makes it possible to run Trans-Canada Air Lines.
I would say to the hon. member for Broadview that I most definitely disagree with him in respect of his observations regarding service in Toronto. I have no doubt that in a city of that size there will be some complaints. Certainly there is not all the service he would like to have or I should like to have; but he knows very well there is a war on. Is he seriously considering that we should again increase the number of deliveries in Toronto at this time? I think not. There are already many deliveries, depending on the districts being served.
I explained to the hon. member some time ago that unfortunately some of our men were off work, because of sickness. They have been replaced by new men. It must be obvious that new men going over routes cannot carry out their duties as rapidly as men who have

been doing the work for a long time, and who have known their routes and their deliveries over a period of years. I would point out another thing to the hon. member, that many of the employees of the Toronto post office have joined the armed forces of this country, and new men have to be broken in to take their places. The men have to learn new routes. There is one other point I might mention, and here the hon. member may not agree with me, but the roads and sidewalks in the city of Toronto have not been conducive to quick delivery. I think it is generally admitted that this has caused delay.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OF INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD-CHANG- ING OF FIXATION-OF-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
Surely not!
Progress reported. '

A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting supplementary estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1942, was presented by Hon. J. L. Ilsley (Minister of Finance), read by Mr. Speaker to the house, and referred to the committee of supply.
What will be the business to-morrow?
The second reading of the war appropriation bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understood that it was
considered desirable to have the wheat matter dealt with and that to-morrow we should go on with the estimates which I have just now moved to be referred to the committee of supply.

My understanding was
that the Prime Minister desired to have the second reading of the war appropriation bill taken so that the bill might get over to the senate. Several weeks have been spent in discussing the resolution stage.
That will be the business to-morrow?

In view of the long discussion there has been of the resolution, I venture to hope that the house will pass the second reading of the bill so that it can be sent over to the senate, and after we have disposed of that, we might take up the legislation to which the Minister of Finance has just referred. I think the house should be prepared to take anything on the order paper, which contains some measures that are not of great importance.

Business of the House

Before we adjourn to-night, can we have an understanding as to what the plan of the government is for proceeding with this whole wheat problem? I understand that the supplementary estimate brought down to-night is to take care of the proposed bonus, but that is only a very small portion of the whole question, and it seems to me that it should not be taken up piecemeal. Of course, I know the government can do what it likes.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The supplementary
estimate is to provide for payments on reductions of wheat acreages under conditions prescribed by the governor in council, for administration expenses in connection therewith, and for temporary appointments that may be required notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act. When that estimate is up for discussion, the whole programme in connection with the making of payments on account of taking acreage out of wheat will be open for discussion, and that is the main part.

Do we understand that there is to be no legislation on the wheat acreage reduction plan, but merely an estimate, and that all the regulations regarding payments will be made by the governor in council? It seems to me that this very important matter should be the subject of legislation, so that the house will have before it in black and white the actual proposals of the government in relation to this great problem.
Hear, hear. Anything else will not be satisfactory.

Absolutely
not.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There are ways in
which the regulations themselves can be brought before the house and discussed. I would suggest that to follow the course now proposed would in all probability result in there being nothing done this year, if we are going to follow the usual process.
I think there can be some cooperation in this matter, but certainly the house should have definitely before it the proposals of the government.

If you
want to get it through, bring down something definite.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is very fond of making just that kind of remark. He has made it on several occasions.

I am
giving a friendly warning.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not a friendly warning. It is a threat to obstruct if we do not proceed in a certain way.

You can interpret it any way you like. The method of procedure which the minister proposes shows the intention to legislate by order in council, and the country will not like it. I do not like it and no other member likes it. Members supporting the government will not like it; the members from Ontario will not like it.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: This is probably not the time to discuss it, but there are two or three ways open for dealing with the question. One w'ay, of course, was to deal with it under the War Measures Act. We did not desire to proceed by that method because it would not have made it possible to have the kind of discussion here that members would want to have. I am quite sure that we can arrange for the kind of discussion and just as full a discussion as hon. members would have if legislation were introduced; and if the house will leave it at that until we come to it to-morrow, or whatever day we do come to it, we can have a full discussion then.
When the question comes before us, does the minister propose to make a statement himself outlining what we may expect if this goes through or will someone else have to make an opening statement?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I would hope to have an opportunity of making a statement.

As a supporter of the government, I believe that this problem should be dealt with by legislation, which offers a much wider opportunity for a full review of the whole problem. It is a matter of great importance.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, March 21, 1941.
